newsitem.title: USA: US Air, Continental post mixed results; TWA has loss.
newsitem.headline: US Air, Continental post mixed results; TWA has loss.

text.p: US Airways Group Inc. and Continental Airlines Inc. reported mixed second-quarter earnings results Wednesday, while Trans World Airlines Inc. posted a bigger-than-expected loss.
US Airways, the nation's sixth largest carrier, said earnings edged up 2 percent in the quarter, but the results failed to meet expectations on Wall Street and its stock fell.
No. 5 Continental said that while pretax earnings set a record in the quarter, net income fell 23 percent. But the results still came in a bit better than expected.

The results did not keep pace with those of the parent companies of United Airlines, the nation's largest carrier, and No. 2 American Airlines, both of which reported better-than-expected results for the quarter.

US Airways, based in Airlington, Va., said net income rose to $206 million in the quarter from $201 million a year earlier. Passenger traffic rose 9 percent, its planes ran with more seats filled and average costs fell, the airline said.

Results for the latest quarter included one-time expenses of $28.3 million related to a restructuring. The earnings equalled $1.92 a share vs. $1.91 a share in 1996, assuming all securities were converted into common stock, which was below forecasts of $2.16 a share for the lastest quarter, according to First Call, which tracks estimates.
US Airways' stock lost $1.50 to $37.375 in consolidated trading on the New York Stock Exchange.

The stock fell even though the airline also said it expected to reach a labour agreement with its pilots after making a new offer in contentious contract talks last week. The airline's disputes with its union employees have hampered its efforts to compete with other carriers.
Sales edged up to $2.2 billion from $2.1 billion.
Continental, based in Houston, said pretax profits of $208 million were the best in its history, but that higher expenses and interest payments reduced net income.
The company said the strong pretax earnings came despite a ticket tax reimposed for the latest quarter and higher fuel prices partly offset by productivity savings and lower aircraft ownership costs.
Net earnings fell 23 percent to $128 million, or $2.01 a share, from $167 million, or $2.53 a share, a year earlier. Sales rose 9 percent to $1.79 billion from $1.64 billion.
The results beat expectations, but Continental stock only edged up 6 cents to $36.44, also on the NYSE.

TWA, still struggling to return to financial health a year after the crash of Flight 800, said operating income tumbled 90 percent in the quarter as passenger traffic fell 9 percent, average fares edged lower and operating expenses rose.

The nation's seventh largest airline reported a loss of $12 million, or 31 cents a share, for the quarter before a one-time charge, compared with a profit of $25.3 million, or 46 cents a share, a year earlier.
Analysts had forecast TWA would lose 23 cents a share before special items, according to First Call, and TWA stock edged down 6 cents to $6.56 on the NYSE.

The carrier's cash position continued to dwindle, falling to about $103 million as of June 30 from $182 million at the end of 1996. Industry analysts said last week that time may be running out for the once-proud airline.
